extracted.intended_audience: Supreme Court justices, appellate judges, patent practitioners, and legal scholars considering 35 U.S.C. §101 issues
extracted.subtask_description: Legal criteria for determining whether method claims (especially diagnostic/medical methods) are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. §101, focusing on claim construction, transformations, and links to physical or tangible objects. The brief applies precedent (Diehr, Benson, Flook, Bilski, Morse, Abele, Classen) to test diagnostic claims involving administering, determining, and observed correlations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-as-a-whole analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: “In determining the eligibility of respondents’ claimed process for patent protection under §101, their claims must be considered as a whole. It is inappropriate to dissect the claims into old and new elements and then to ignore the presence of the old elements in the analysis.” (Diamond v. Diehr cited)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not isolate a single step (e.g., an 'observed correlation') and evaluate only that piece for §101. Consider the combination of steps (including conventional or well-known steps) because a new combination of steps may be patentable even if constituents were known. The brief applies this to diagnostic claims: include 'administering' and 'determining' steps in the §101 inquiry even when those steps are well-known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation/reduction test (machine-or-transformation clue)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Transformation and reduction of an article ‘to a different state or thing’ is the clue to the patentability of a process claim that does not include particular machines.” (Gottschalk v. Benson cited)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A process claim that effects a physical/chemical/electrical transformation of an article is an indicator of §101 eligibility. For diagnostic methods, transformations of body chemistry (through administering drugs or extracting/metabolite determination) may satisfy this clue. But the existence of a transformation is a clue, not an automatic rule of patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution / post-solution activity rule
rubrics_metrics.description: “The notion that post-solution activity, no matter how conventional or obvious in itself, can transform an unpatentable principle into a patentable process is false.” (Parker v. Flook cited; Diehr discussion)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding conventional or token steps (e.g., 'apply to surveying techniques' or routine data-gathering) to an abstract idea, law of nature, or mathematical formula does not make the claim patentable. Courts should identify and disregard insignificant post-solution activity when it is merely a drafting device to claim an unpatentable principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centrality of transformative steps (not token extra-solution activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transformative steps that are central/essential to the claim (i.e., not 'token extra-solution activity') must be considered and can support patent eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether recited transformative steps (e.g., 'administering' a drug, 'determining' metabolite levels) actually contribute meaningful limitations and practical application, rather than merely gather information. Central transformative steps that generate data applied to enable a practical adjustment (e.g., drug dosage change) weigh in favor of §101 eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical link to a specific physical/tangible object
rubrics_metrics.description: A clue to patentability is whether claim steps have a 'physical' link to (i.e., manipulate) a specific physical or tangible object (e.g., manipulating blood chemistry, loading a mold, opening a press). (Diehr, Corning, Tilghman examples)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed steps physically manipulate or transform a real-world thing (including physical phenomena like electrical signals or chemical properties), that connection supports patent eligibility. For diagnostics, 'administering' and 'determining' that manipulate blood chemistry provide such a physical link.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtual link: manipulation of data representing physical objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Manipulating data that represent a specific physical or tangible object (a 'virtual link') can be sufficient for patent-eligibility. (O’Reilly v. Morse; In re Abele cited)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that transform or manipulate data tied to real-world physical objects (e.g., CT X‑ray attenuation data representing bones; data tagged with dosage indicators) create a virtual link to those objects and may be patentable. The claim must tie the data to the particular physical object or representation, not to abstract or generic data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding preemption of laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim must be tailored so it does not preempt the fundamental principle itself; it must encompass only a particular application rather than all uses of the principle. ('Claims that are close to ‘laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas’ ... do not count as ‘processes’ under §101.') (Diehr, Bilski discussions)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claim, considered as a whole and excluding insignificant extra-solution activity, would preempt all practical uses of a natural law/phenomenon or abstract idea. If it would, the claim likely fails §101. Narrowly tie claims to specific applications or transformations to avoid preemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter patentability filter (Classen): practical application vs mere data-gathering
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all transformative steps suffice; courts should apply a 'subject matter patentability filter' to distinguish transformations that merely gather data for a body of knowledge from those that put knowledge to a practical use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Classen, transforming steps that only collect data (for later comparison or to build knowledge) may be insufficient, whereas transformations that enable a practical application (e.g., generating a subject-specific regimen used in a subsequent implementation step) are likely patent-eligible. Evaluate claim order and how the transformative step is used (before/after comparison, whether it enables later action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diehr principle for formulas implemented in structure/process
rubrics_metrics.description: When a mathematical formula is implemented or applied in a structure or process that, considered as a whole, performs a function the patent laws protect (e.g., transforming or reducing an article to a different state or thing), the claim satisfies §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an otherwise abstract formula is integrated into a practical process that effects a tangible transformation or control of physical apparatus (e.g., software that signals a device to open a press), the claim can be patent-eligible. Mere limitation to a technological environment without meaningful integration is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish §101 from §§102/103 (novelty/obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether individual steps of a claim are 'well-known' may be relevant to novelty (§102) or obviousness (§103), but does not by itself determine whether §101 is satisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a §101 inquiry, do not conflate knownness of claim elements with subject-matter eligibility; assess eligibility under §101 first via claim-as-a-whole, transformation/links, and preemption analysis, and leave novelty/obviousness defenses to §§102/103 analysis.
